title: Does O C still bisect the angle if the arcs meet on the far side?
description: A question from the book asks what happens if the two equal arcs are drawn on the other side of the corner. The arcs meet outside the angle, the same congruent triangles still work, and the line through the corner, extended, still bisects the angle.
teaching_notes: One idea: the SSS argument does not care on which side the arcs meet, and the opposite ray makes equal supplementary angles. Watch for students who think the bisector must lie inside the angle's arc region.

video_script.why: The child has met the meeting point inside the angle and has not yet asked what happens when equal arcs meet on the other side of the corner.
video_script.substitution: The construction is done in the same way as the example in the book, with the equal arcs drawn on the far side of the corner, and the same triangles explain the result.
video_script.anchor: If equal arcs from A and B meet at a point C on the far side of the corner O, will the line O C still be an angle bisector?
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, the line C O extended still bisects the angle

final_answer.value: Yes. OA = OB, AC = BC and OC is common, so ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS and ∠AOC = ∠BOC; their supplements are equal too, so the line CO, extended beyond O, still bisects ∠AOB
final_answer.spoken: yes, the line C O extended still bisects the angle, because the triangles are congruent by side side side and the supplementary angles are equal

never_show: the answer yes before the answer line
maths_rules: Mark A and B on the arms with OA = OB.
A radius larger than OA, with arcs from A and from B on the far side of O, meets at C: AC = BC.
Triangle OAC is congruent to triangle OBC by SSS (OA = OB, AC = BC, OC common), so angle AOC = angle BOC.
Extend CO beyond O to D inside angle AOB. Angle AOD + angle AOC = 180 degrees and angle BOD + angle BOC = 180 degrees.
Angle AOD = 180 degrees minus angle AOC and angle BOD = 180 degrees minus angle BOC, and these are equal, so OD bisects angle AOB.
video_script.design: One idea: the same SSS pair works when C is outside the angle, and equal angles have equal supplements. The line CO, extended past O, is the bisector.
